## Digital Marketing Agency in Pune: How to Get More Google Reviews Legitimately and Respond to Them (Without Risking Your Business Profile)

The legitimate way to get more Google reviews is to ask every genuine customer, at the moment they are most satisfied, using Google's own review link or QR code, with no reward, no filtering of who gets asked and no instruction about what to write. Then reply to every review, good or bad, in a calm and specific way. That is the whole method. Everything else in this guide is detail about doing it consistently, and about avoiding the shortcuts that Google's policies prohibit. If you are choosing a digital marketing agency in Pune, the most useful test is whether it is willing to work within those rules or whether it offers to "get you 100 reviews this month".

This article is written for owners of Pune service businesses such as clinics, coaching classes, interior designers, CA firms, salons, repair services and small agencies. For them a Google Business Profile is often the first thing a prospect sees, and its reviews decide whether the phone rings. We cover what Google's policies say, how to ask without crossing a line, how to answer reviews, how to handle fake or unfair ones, and what to ask an agency. We do not quote statistics on how reviews change conversions, because we have not found a source we trust for Indian local businesses. Where a number matters, we say where it comes from or mark it as unknown.

If your profile is already suspended or you suspect it may be, read our guide to [recovering from a Google Business Profile suspension](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-business-profile-suspension-2026/) first. Review manipulation is one of the reasons profiles are actioned, which is why this topic deserves care.

## What Google's review policy actually says

Google publishes its rules for user-contributed content in its Maps policy pages. Read the source rather than relying on an agency's summary, because the rules are short and they are the ones that will be applied to your profile. The points below are drawn from Google's [Maps user-contributed content policy on prohibited and restricted content](https://support.google.com/contributionpolicy/answer/7400114), and we have kept the wording close to the original.

### Fake engagement

Google states that fake engagement is not allowed and will be removed. Its examples include paid or in-kind reviews and one person posting from multiple accounts. Merchants and users also may not solicit content that is not genuine, offer incentives for reviews, or post on a competitor's listing to damage it. If a vendor writes the reviews, or arranges for people who never used your service to write them, that is fake engagement no matter how natural the text sounds.

### Incentivized or biased reviews

Reviews posted because of an incentive from the business are classed by Google as rating manipulation and are removed. The policy covers incentives offered in exchange for writing a review and also incentives offered in exchange for changing or removing one. A free consultation, a discount on the next visit, a coupon, a lucky draw entry or a small gift all count as incentives. Google's [guidance on reviews](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122) repeats this: you may ask customers to leave a review through a link or QR code, but you may not offer free or discounted goods or services in exchange.

Unusual volumes or patterns of reviews intended to shift a rating are also treated as manipulation. That matters because a sudden burst of reviews on a profile that previously had very few is exactly what a purchased batch looks like.

### Review gating and selective solicitation

This is the rule that catches well-meaning businesses. Google's policy says merchants may not discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively solicit positive ones. In practice, review gating means a flow such as: ask the customer "How was your experience?", send happy customers to Google and unhappy customers to a private feedback form. It feels sensible, because you want to hear complaints privately. But the Google link then reaches only the people you pre-selected as satisfied, which is selective solicitation.

The policy also says businesses should not pressure customers to leave reviews on the premises, require specific content, or ask staff to collect a set number of reviews. It allows merchants to encourage genuine reviews as long as they offer no incentive and do not try to influence the rating or content.

So the safe pattern is simple. If you ask for feedback at all, ask everyone the same way and give everyone the same route to Google. You can offer a private feedback channel as an additional option for anyone who prefers it, but you cannot use it as a filter.

### Conflicts of interest

Content from people with a conflict of interest is a violation. Google's examples include current or former employees, people with a contractual or consulting relationship with the business, and others with professional or personal ties, including competitors and family members. For a small Pune business that means your staff, your relatives and your agency's employees should not review you. It is a common slip: an owner asks the team to "post a good review for the office", and the burst of reviews comes from accounts linked to people who work there.

## How reviews relate to local visibility, and what Google does not say

Business owners are often told that reviews are a ranking factor. Here is exactly what Google says. In its guide to [improving your local ranking](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091), Google says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and prominence. Prominence is described as how well known a business is, and Google lists the number of reviews and the ratings as inputs to it. The page says that more reviews and positive ratings can help your local ranking, and that positive reviews and helpful replies can help your business stand out. It also says there is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking.

Three conclusions follow, and none of them needs an invented statistic.

- Reviews are one input, not the whole picture. Relevance (how complete and accurate your profile is) and distance (how far you are from the searcher) matter too, and you cannot change the second one.
- Google's own wording is "can help". It does not publish a formula, a target number of reviews or a weight. An agency that promises a specific ranking position from a specific number of reviews is guessing.
- Reviews shape the decision after the click. Google's review guidance says reviews appear next to your profile in Maps and Search and help people decide. For a clinic or a repair shop, a recent, detailed set of reviews with owner replies often matters more to the enquiry than a one-position change in ranking.

If you want to understand how the map results fit with the rest of your search presence, our article on [local SEO and the Google map pack in Pune](/blog/local-seo-google-map-pack-pune-2026/) covers the wider picture. Reviews are one chapter of it.

## Setting up before you ask

A few preparations make the asking itself much easier and more effective.

### Make sure the profile is verified and the details are correct

Google notes that you need to verify your business before you can reply to reviews. Check that your name, address, phone number, hours and categories match what you display on your website and signage. Mismatches cause confusion for customers and, in the worst case, attract the attention of Google's quality checks.

### Create the review link and QR code from Google

Google's help describes a way to create a link or QR code to request reviews, and a manual route as well: search for your business on Google Maps, open Reviews, and use the Share review option to copy a link. Use the official link, not a third-party redirect that might filter or route users. Test it on a phone that is not signed in as the owner, because the reviewer must be signed in to a Google Account to post, and you want to know what a customer sees.

## How to ask for a Google review ethically

The most reliable principle is to ask everyone who finished a service with you, using the same words and the same link, shortly after the service. The details below are practical ways to do it.

### Pick the moment

Ask when the customer has just received the value: the treatment is finished, the design is handed over, the repair works, the course batch has completed a module. A request sent two weeks later is easy to ignore. A request made while the customer is still thanking you is easy to act on.

### Choose a channel the customer already uses

- **In person with a QR code.** A small printed card or a QR code on the reception counter or invoice. Google's policy warns against pressuring customers on the premises, so offer the code politely and let the customer decide; do not stand next to them while they type.
- **WhatsApp after the service.** For many Pune customers, a short WhatsApp message is the natural channel. If you contact customers on WhatsApp, follow the rules about consent: the customer should have given a phone number for service communication, and a request for a review is a business message, not a casual chat. Our checklist on [WhatsApp opt-in compliance](/blog/whatsapp-opt-in-compliance-checklist/) explains what is needed before you send business messages at scale.
### Write a request that does not steer

A good request thanks the customer, says that honest feedback helps others decide, and gives the link. It does not ask for five stars, does not suggest what to write, and does not mention a reward. Compare these two.

| Request wording | Why it works or fails |
|---|---|
| "Thank you for choosing us. If you have a minute, an honest review on Google helps other people find the right clinic. Link: …" | Neutral, same for everyone, no incentive. Acceptable. |
| "Please give us a 5-star review and get 10% off your next visit." | Asks for a rating and offers an incentive. Breaches the policy twice. |
| "If you were happy, review us on Google. If not, tell us here." | Review gating: only the happy are sent to Google. Breaches the policy on selective solicitation. |
| "Our target is 20 reviews this month, please help the team." | Staff or customers pressured to meet a number. Avoid. |

## A worked example (hypothetical)

The following is an illustration, not a real client. The numbers are chosen only to show the arithmetic of a routine.

A hypothetical physiotherapy clinic in Pune sees about 25 new patients a week and has 40 Google reviews. The owner decides on a simple routine: the front desk keeps a printed QR card at reception, and a WhatsApp message with the same neutral wording and Google link goes to every patient who completes a course of sessions. Patients who finish a course are a smaller group than weekly new patients, so assume about 10 a week.

If, hypothetically, one in five of those 10 patients posts a review, the clinic gains roughly two reviews a week, or around 8-9 a month. Over six months that is around 50 genuine reviews added to the 40 already there. The one-in-five figure is an assumption for this illustration, not a benchmark; your own response rate may be lower or higher, and the way to learn it is to count requests sent and reviews received for two months.

What matters more than the arithmetic is what the owner does not do: the clinic does not filter patients by satisfaction, does not offer a discount, does not ask staff to post and does not buy a bundle. When a patient posts a two-star review about waiting time, the owner replies politely, and the reply itself becomes part of the clinic's public record of how it treats feedback.

## How to reply to reviews

Google recommends replying to reviews, positive and negative, and says a reply shows customers that their feedback matters. Some mechanics from Google's help: the reviewer is notified when you reply, they can change their review afterwards, and if they do the review's date updates. Replies are checked against Google's content policies, are public, and appear as being from the business, not from your personal name. You can edit or delete your own reply later.

### Principles for every reply

1. **Reply promptly.** Aim for a reply within a couple of working days. Google advises replying promptly to negative reviews.
2. **Be specific.** Mention something from the review so it is clear a person read it.
3. **Keep it short.** Three or four sentences. The reply is read by future customers, not only by the reviewer.
4. **Never reveal private information.** Do not confirm that the reviewer was a patient or client, do not mention treatment details, amounts or documents. Confidentiality matters most for clinics, law and accounting practices.
5. **Do not argue.** You can disagree politely with facts, but the audience is the next customer.
6. **Do not offer compensation in the reply for changing the review.** Google treats incentives for revising or removing a review as manipulation.

### Reply templates you can adapt

**For a positive review:**
"Thank you for the kind words, and for mentioning the clear explanation of the work plan. Our team will be glad to hear it. If anything comes up later, we are a call away. — The management team"

**For a negative review with a real problem:**
"We are sorry that your experience fell short, and thank you for telling us. We would like to understand what happened and put it right if we can. Please call our office on [number] or message us on WhatsApp so we can look into it. — The management team"

## Fake, unfair and unwanted reviews

### Know the difference between negative and violating

A negative review is not a policy violation. A review that says the clinic was late and the staff were rude is the reviewer's experience. A review is potentially removable when it breaks the policy, for example if it contains fake engagement, is posted by a competitor, a former employee or someone with a conflict of interest, is off-topic, or is obviously not based on a real visit. Google's help says business owners can flag reviews they think violate content policies. Its page on managing reviews does not say that owners can delete customer reviews, and you should not expect it to happen on request.

### The practical flagging routine

1. Open your profile's reviews and identify the specific policy that applies. Be ready to say which one.
2. Use Google's report option for that review, following Google's help article on reporting inappropriate reviews.
3. Take a screenshot and note the date, in case you need to follow up.
4. Reply publicly, professionally, whether or not the flag succeeds, because customers read the reply.
5. If a pattern of fake reviews appears, with several from new accounts in a short period, document it and escalate through Google Business Profile support rather than flagging repeatedly in the same hour.

We do not state how long a flag takes or what proportion succeed, because Google's pages we reviewed do not say, and we have no source for it. Plan as if the review will remain, and reply for the sake of the readers.

## Handling reviews in a multi-staff business

When several people deal with customers, reviews often name individuals. A few habits keep this healthy.

- **Give one person ownership of replies.** They can consult others, but one voice avoids contradicting messages.
- **Keep staff and relatives from reviewing.** Because of the conflict of interest rule, ask the team not to post reviews for the business, even if their intentions are good.
- **Log recurring complaints.** If three reviews mention the same waiting-room delay, fix the delay. This is the part of review management that actually changes outcomes.

If your business has more than one location, each location is its own profile with its own reviews, and processes need to be consistent. Our article on [local SEO for multi-location businesses in India](/blog/local-seo-multi-location-businesses-india/) covers the structure.

## What to ask a digital marketing agency about reviews

When you evaluate agencies, a handful of questions separates the careful ones from the risky ones.

1. **"How will you help us get more reviews?"** A good answer describes a request process, a link or QR code, templates and training for your team. A bad answer promises a number of reviews by a date.
2. **"Do you ever write, buy or post reviews on our behalf?"** The only acceptable answer is no. Google lists paid reviews as prohibited fake engagement.
3. **"Will customers be filtered by satisfaction before they see the Google link?"** The answer should be no, because of the review gating rule.
4. **"Who owns the Google Business Profile and the review link?"** The owner should be you, with the agency as a manager.
5. **"How do you reply to negative reviews, and who approves replies?"** You should see a draft process in which a person from your business approves anything involving customer details.
6. **"How fast will enquiries be answered?"** Reviews bring people in; slow replies lose them. See our [lead response workflow guide](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-lead-response-speed-follow-up-workflow-2026/).
7. **"What will you report?"** A sensible report covers requests sent, reviews received, average rating, reply time and calls or direction requests from the profile, not a vanity count. Our guide to [retainer deliverables and reporting](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-retainer-deliverables-reporting-2026/) lists what a monthly report should contain.

### Red flags

- A price per review, or "guaranteed" review packages.
- A promise of a ranking position, or of removing negative reviews.
- Reviews arriving in bursts from accounts with no history.
- An agency that asks for your personal Google password rather than manager access.
- A tool that sends only happy customers to Google.
- Staff reviewing "to get things started".

If any of those appear, you risk losing the profile, and the cost of recovering it is far higher than the cost of earning reviews slowly. Review manipulation is also one of the causes of the suspensions we describe in our [suspension recovery guide](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-business-profile-suspension-2026/).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is it allowed to ask customers for Google reviews?

Yes. Google's guidance says you can ask customers to leave a review by sharing a Google link or QR code. What you cannot do is offer free or discounted goods or services in exchange, or selectively ask only the customers you expect to be positive.

### Can I give a discount to customers who leave a review?

No. Google treats incentivized reviews as rating manipulation and removes them, and the same applies to incentives offered for changing or removing a review. If you want to thank customers, do it for everyone who completes a service, independent of whether they post a review.

### Can I delete a bad Google review?

Not directly. Google's help describes flagging a review that you believe violates its content policies, and does not say that owners can delete customer reviews. For a review that is simply negative, reply politely and, where possible, fix the problem it describes.

### Do more Google reviews improve local ranking?

Google says that more reviews and positive ratings can help your local ranking, alongside relevance and distance, and it says there is no way to pay for a better ranking. It does not publish a number of reviews or a formula, so treat any promise of a specific position with caution.

Sources: [Google Maps user-contributed content policy: prohibited and restricted content](https://support.google.com/contributionpolicy/answer/7400114); [Google Business Profile Help: Read and reply to reviews](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122); [Google Business Profile Help: Tips to improve your local ranking](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091); [Google Business Profile Help: Manage reviews (reply, edit reply, flag)](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474050). Hypothetical figures in the worked example are illustrative assumptions, not benchmarks.
